Investor guide

Duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes in the GTA

Multi-unit homes can pay their own way, if the units are legal. Here's what's permitted and what to check.

Ali Bayat
Figures checked against the sources below on November 21, 2026
Published November 21, 2026
3-minute readFor investorsToronto & York Region

01What's permitted

4 unitsToronto, citywideMultiplexes permitted as of right in low-rise neighbourhoods
6 unitsParts of TorontoToronto & East York district and Ward 23; in force since 2025
3 unitsMost of OntarioOn serviced residential lots, under the Planning Act

02How unit count changes things

Duplex

2 units

  • Insured with 5% down if you live in one unit
  • Often a house with a legal second suite
  • Simplest to manage

Triplex

3 units

  • 10% minimum down if you live in it
  • Fire separation and code rules get stricter
  • More rent, more management

Fourplex

4 units

  • Largest size still financed as residential
  • 10% down owner-occupied, 20% if not
  • Check zoning, parking and permits closely

03Verify before you count the rent

  • Permits and final inspectionsFor each unit, from the city's building department.
  • Zoning for that addressPermissions vary; check the specific lot.
  • Fire separations and exitsRequired between units; costly to add later.
  • Existing leasesRents, start dates, and whether units are under the rent guideline.
  • Separate metersWho pays utilities changes your expenses.
  • InsuranceConfirm the insurer knows the number of units.

04Red flags in listings

  • "Potential" or "in-law" suiteUsually means it isn't a legal unit.
  • No permits on file for a basement apartmentYou inherit the risk.
  • Rents far above comparablesAsk for leases and payment history.
Ali's take

Ask for permits before you ask for rents. A legal fourplex and a house with three unpermitted units are different investments at the same price.
